newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK shares off slightly, Bangkok continues slide.
newsitem.headline: HK shares off slightly, Bangkok continues slide.

text.p: Hong Kong shares fell back marginally on Thursday on profit-taking after the previous session's record high close, brokers said.
Elsewhere, the battered Bangkok bourse shed 1.73 percent to close at its lowest level in more than three years, but Bombay was up three percent.
Tokyo and Taipei were closed for public holidays.

Hong Kong's key Hang Seng Index eased 8.10 points or 0.07 percent to close at 12,242.47, just shy of Wednesday's record of 12,250.57, as profit-takers targeted the market's better performers, brokers said.
Turnover remained high at HK$7.86 billion (US$1.01 billion), well above Wednesday's HK$6.21 billion.
"Volume is huge. There is good liquidity in the system right now," said James Robertson, head of Hong Kong sales at Salomon Brothers.
""A good degree of interest is being created in the U.S. for this market," Robertson said.

Bangkok's bourse, which fell six percent on Monday, lost 16.44 points to 933.00 after investors sold property, finance and bank stocks on rumours that a property developing firm was facing cash problems, brokers said.
A senior official at Thailand's Finance Ministry told reporters earlier in the week the market was likely to remain volatile until a new government is formed after general elections on November 17.
Thursday's close was the lowest since July 30, 1993, when it was 928.20.
"The market sentiment was poor today on rumours that a property firm was having cash problems. The rumours induced investors to sell property stocks," said Thanawat Patchimkul of Seamico Securities.
Traders in Bombay said bids from funds and speculators, propelled Bombay's benchmark stocks index to close 2.92 percent higher, up 88.71 points to 3126.34.
Prices rose on heavy short covering by punters in Calcutta and Bombay and selected bids by foreign and local funds.
"Everything was heavily oversold and some correction had to come. Some buying from Indian insitutions has helped to prop up sentiment," said a trader at a foreign brokerage.
Anticipation of lower interest rates pushed the Seoul stock market to a higher close for the fifth straight session.
The composite index defied a brief spell of profit-taking to end up 12.43 points or 1.52 percent at a provisional 830.21.

"The market is widely reflecting investors' hopes of a cut in interest rates, which will favourably affect corporate profitability and their export competitiveness," said Ahn Hyo-moon, fund manager of Korea Investment Trust Co.

Brokers said many investors now believe the nation's economy has hit rock-bottom, given a reduced stockpile in the steel, petrochemical and semiconductor sectors. "This has spurred active rotational buying interest across the board," Kim said.
The Australian share market finished firmer with blue chips reversing early falls after a weaker-than-expected September jobs report spurred renewed speculation about a near-term interest rate cut.
The benchmark All Ordinaries index closed 12.8 points higher, or 0.55 percent, at 2,323.5.
Brokers said the weak employment data moved currency and bond markets and kicked life into equities which had drifted lower on light volume before the figures were released.
New Zealand's share market suffered a bout of pre-election nerves, led down by market heavyweight Telecom, the stock seen most vulnerable to a change of government.
The top 40 index fell 1.17 percent or 26.31 points to 2231.71.
Brokers said Telecom had been a political target of parties wanting to trim the level of its profits and limit foreign ownership. Ameritech and Bell Atlantic each own a quarter of Telecom.
At 11.51 GMT, the dollar was at 111.37/1.47 yen and 1.5310/20 marks.
Bullion ended at US$381.40/70, against New York's US$381.05/55 close.
SIMEX North Sea November Brent crude oil futures fell five cents in late trading to $24.22 against London's settlement of $24.27.
